---
title: "seqbench: Anytime-Valid Sequential Benchmarking of Algorithms in R"
date: "2026-10-23"
abstract: >
  Algorithm comparisons are run as sequential experiments: results are inspected as instances are solved, budgets are adapted and the study stops when the outcome looks settled. Fixed-sample tests lose their guarantees under this use. The \pkg{seqbench} package maintains a confidence sequence for the mean paired difference of losses, valid at data-dependent stopping times, and reads it against a pre-registered margin of practical equivalence. It declares one algorithm relevantly better, the two equivalent, or the comparison inconclusive within its budget, all at one error level. In a simulation study with 2,000 replications per cell, the distribution-free boundaries never exceeded 0.45% false declarations, while a repeatedly inspected t-test reached 38%; a Gaussian confidence sequence given the true variance needed 1.4 to 21 times fewer instances. Applications to vehicle routing heuristics, vaccination strategies on contact networks and community detection show the workflow and its costs.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Algorithm comparisons in optimisation, machine learning, operations research and
computational statistics are rarely fixed-sample experiments. Instances are run in batches;
intermediate results are inspected; more instances are added where the outcome looks close;
the study stops when one method "clearly" dominates or when the budget runs out. Each of these
habits invalidates a fixed-sample test. Inspecting a $t$-test after every instance and stopping
at the first rejection inflates the type-I error without bound [@armitage1969]; the simulation
study of [Section 5](#sec-sim) measures `r pct(mx("seqbench:naive_fixed"), 0)` false declarations at
a nominal 5% in one of its scenarios. The problem is old and well understood in clinical
trials, but the benchmarking literature mostly ignores it. Best-practice guides recommend
statistical tests [@bartz2020; @eimer2025] but not sequential ones, and the racing methods used
in algorithm configuration [@birattari2002; @lopezibanez2016] inspect repeatedly by design
without controlling the error of the final comparison.

The statistical tool that repairs this is the confidence sequence [@howard2021; @ramdas2023]:
a sequence of sets $C_t$ with $P(\forall t \ge 1: \mu \in C_t) \ge 1-\alpha$, which remains
valid at every data-dependent stopping time. @waudbysmith2024 give tight confidence sequences
for the mean of bounded random variables by betting; @choe2024 use confidence sequences to
compare two forecasters; @arnold2026 build sequential model confidence sets. In R,
\CRANpkg{safestats} [@safestats; @ly2024] implements anytime-valid $t$-tests and their
confidence sequences, and \CRANpkg{seqcomp} [@seqcomp] compares probabilistic forecasts
sequentially.

\CRANpkg{seqbench} packages this machinery into a *protocol for benchmarking two algorithms*.
Its contributions are practical rather than methodological: an explicit population estimand;
pairing by instance with seeds treated as a cluster; a pre-registered margin of practical
equivalence turned into a three-way decision rule that inherits the error control of the
confidence sequence; cost accounting, with an inconclusive outcome that is never converted
into a decision; and a result contract that reports what was assumed and what was consumed.
We are explicit about what this does not buy. The error control is a margin rule applied to an
existing confidence sequence, and, as [Section 5](#sec-sim) shows, the distribution-free
boundaries pay a substantial price in instances relative to a Gaussian sequence that knows the
variance. The package makes that price visible.

[Section 2](#sec-setting) states the problem and its assumptions, [Section 3](#sec-protocol)
the protocol and its guarantee, [Section 4](#sec-package) the package, [Section
5](#sec-sim) the simulation study and [Section 6](#sec-apps) three applications.
[Section 7](#sec-uses) discusses where the protocol applies, and [Section
8](#sec-limitations) its limitations.

# The comparison as a sequential experiment {#sec-setting}

## Estimand

Let $P$ be a population of problem instances and $S$ a distribution of seeds (random restarts,
initialisations, stochastic replications). Running algorithm $k \in \{A, B\}$ on instance $i$
with seed $s$ yields a loss $L_k(i, s)$, smaller being better; the loss is the user's choice
and the package does not interpret it. The paired difference is
$D(i, s) = L_A(i, s) - L_B(i, s)$, and the estimand is the population mean

$$\mu = E_{i \sim P}\big[E_{s \sim S}[D(i, s)]\big].$$

A negative $\mu$ favours A. This is what "A is better than B on problems like these" means. It
is not the mean over a fixed benchmark suite, a finite-population target for which sequential
inference would sample without replacement [@waudbysmith2020], nor a probability of winning;
both are legitimate targets and neither is addressed here.

## Practical relevance

A margin $\delta > 0$, in loss units, is fixed before any data are seen and partitions the
parameter space into three hypotheses that cover the real line (Table \@ref(tab:tab1)).

```{r tab1}
tab <- data.frame(
  Hypothesis = c("$H_A$", "$H_0$", "$H_B$"),
  Condition = c("$\\mu < -\\delta$", "$|\\mu| \\le \\delta$", "$\\mu > \\delta$"),
  Reading = c("A is relevantly better", "practically equivalent", "B is relevantly better"))
knitr::kable(tab, caption = "The three hypotheses defined by the margin.", escape = FALSE,
             row.names = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

The margin is a domain decision (one percentage point of accuracy, one percentage point of
optimality gap, one percentage point of a population infected), recorded with the design and
never tuned after inspection. This is the reading of a confidence interval used by
equivalence testing [@schuirmann1987; @lakens2017] and by Bayesian regions of practical
equivalence [@benavoli2017], made anytime-valid.

## Assumptions {#sec-assumptions}

- **(A1) Independent instances.** Instances are drawn independently from $P$, and the order in
  which they are run does not depend on their losses.
- **(A2) Seeds fixed by design.** The number of seeds of an instance and their values are
  chosen without looking at any loss of that instance; seeds are drawn from $S$.
- **(A3) Bounded losses.** Both losses lie in a known interval $[\ell_{lo}, \ell_{hi}]$, so
  $D \in [a, b] = [\ell_{lo} - \ell_{hi}, \ell_{hi} - \ell_{lo}]$.
- **(A4) No adaptive reuse.** An instance whose losses were observed does not receive new seeds
  and does not reappear.

Let $\bar D_t$ be the seed-averaged difference of the $t$-th instance and
$X_t = (\bar D_t - a)/(b - a) \in [0, 1]$. Under (A1)--(A4),
$E[X_t \mid \mathcal F_{t-1}] = \nu = 1/2 + \mu/(b-a)$ for every $t$, where
$\mathcal F_{t-1}$ contains everything observed before instance $t$: the instance is a fresh
draw from $P$ (A1), and given the instance its seeds are fresh draws from $S$ whose number may
depend on the past but not on the instance's own losses (A2). This conditional-mean condition
is all the confidence sequences below require. The $X_t$ need not be identically distributed
(the number of seeds may vary), and arbitrary dependence between the two algorithms, and across
the seeds of an instance, is allowed. (A4) is what makes (A2) enforceable: adding seeds to an
instance after seeing its losses makes $X_t$ depend on its own outcome. The sequential unit is
therefore the instance, not the evaluation.

Timeouts and failed runs must be resolved before the data reach the package. A penalised
outcome [PAR-$k$, the cutoff time times $k$ for unfinished runs, @hutter2009] keeps the loss
bounded and changes the estimand to the mean penalised loss; censoring keeps the estimand and
breaks boundedness. The package takes the first route and records the choice as the user's.
Truncating an unbounded loss at a cutoff is the same kind of choice, and it also changes the
estimand. Where a bound holds by construction, as for the relative gap to a lower bound or an
attack rate ([Section 6](#sec-apps)), no such choice is needed.

# The protocol and its guarantee {#sec-protocol}

## Confidence sequences for bounded means

On the $[0, 1]$ scale the package offers three confidence sequences of @waudbysmith2024, all
with the time-uniform guarantee under the conditional-mean condition above: the
predictable-plug-in Hoeffding sequence (deterministic width; distribution-free and very
conservative), the predictable-plug-in empirical-Bernstein sequence (variance-adaptive) and the
hedged betting sequence (the default and the tightest of the three). A fourth valid option,
`"bernstein_declared"`, is a predictable-plug-in Bennett sequence that takes a declared upper
bound on the standard deviation of the paired difference; its coverage holds only if the
declaration is true, and the declaration is recorded in the result as a fifth assumption. A
last option, `"naive_fixed"`, is the fixed-sample $t$ interval recomputed after every instance.
It is *not* a confidence sequence, is flagged invalid in every output, and exists only as the
negative control of [Section 5](#sec-sim). Because every set of one confidence sequence
contains $\nu$ on the same event, the running intersection $C_t^\cap = \bigcap_{s \le t} C_s$
is again a $1-\alpha$ confidence sequence, and the decision rule uses it.

## Decision rule {#sec-rule}

With $C_t^\cap = [L_t, U_t]$ mapped back to loss units, the rules are checked in this order
after each instance:

1. inconclusive, with reason `cs_empty`, if $C_t^\cap$ is empty (an event of probability at
   most $\alpha$; never a decision);
2. A is relevantly better if $U_t < -\delta$;
3. B is relevantly better if $L_t > \delta$;
4. practically equivalent if $-\delta \le L_t$ and $U_t \le \delta$;
5. otherwise continue, unless the budget or the maximum number of instances is exhausted, in
   which case the outcome is inconclusive, with reason `budget` or `n_max`.

**Proposition (no false declaration, one $\alpha$).** Let $(C_t)$ be a $1-\alpha$ confidence
sequence for $\nu$ and let the procedure stop at the first declaration or at an arbitrary
stopping time $\tau$, possibly driven by the budget. Then the probability that it issues a
false declaration, of any of the three kinds, is at most $\alpha$.

*Proof.* On the event $E = \{\forall t: \nu \in C_t\}$, which has probability at least
$1-\alpha$, $\nu \in C_t^\cap$, hence $L_t \le \nu \le U_t$, for every $t$. Each declaration
condition then implies the corresponding hypothesis ($U_t < -\delta$ implies $\mu < -\delta$,
and so on), so every declaration issued on $E$ is correct, whenever it is issued. The event
of a false declaration is therefore contained in $E^c$. $\square$

The proof is one paragraph because the confidence sequence does the work. What the protocol
adds is the reading: the three declarations are events on one simultaneous confidence set, so
no split of $\alpha$ is needed (two one-sided tests for equivalence need none either, being an
intersection--union test), and the guarantee holds at the data-dependent time at which a
benchmarker actually stops. "Inconclusive" carries no error: it is the complement of a
declaration, and its probability is a design quantity.

## Planning {#sec-planning}

For the Hoeffding sequence the half-width $w_t$ is deterministic. On the coverage event a
comparison run with that boundary has issued the correct declaration by
$t^*(g) = \min\{t : 2 w_t < g\}$, where $g$ is the distance from $\nu$ to the nearest threshold
on the $[0,1]$ scale; $t^*$ depends only on $(\alpha, \delta, \text{bounds})$ and a target
distance, and `planning_horizon()` returns it. The guarantee is distribution-free but belongs
to the Hoeffding boundary, and it is very conservative: at $\delta = 0.02$, bounds $[0, 1]$ and
a distance of 0.02, $t^* =$ `r num(planning_horizon(comparison_design(margin = 0.02, bounds = c(0, 1)), 0.02))`
instances, against a median of `r num(base$median_n[base$method == "seqbench:betting" & base$mu == 0 & base$h < 0.1])`
for the betting boundary in the corresponding cell of [Section 5](#sec-sim). Given a planning
value of the standard deviation of the paired difference, `planning_horizon()` returns instead
the horizon of the empirical-Bernstein width with that variance plugged in. This is an
approximation, not a bound. In the regimes of [Section 5](#sec-sim) the median stopping time
was about one half of it for the empirical-Bernstein boundary and about one quarter for the
betting boundary; the truncated-bet analysis there explains why.

# The package {#sec-package}

## Workflow

```{r workflow, echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
library(seqbench)
set.seed(1)
design <- comparison_design(alpha = 0.05, margin = 0.02, bounds = c(0, 1),
                            boundary = "betting", budget = 800)
state  <- initialize_comparison(design)

# one row per (instance, seed); here A loses 0.05 more than B on average
la <- runif(400, 0.40, 0.80)
losses <- data.frame(instance = 1:400, seed = 1L, loss_a = la,
                     loss_b = la - 0.05 + runif(400, -0.17, 0.17))
state  <- update_comparison(state, losses)
stopping_decision(state)
```

```{r workflow2, echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
glance(state)
```

`update_comparison()` is incremental: rows of new instances can be fed at any time and in any
batch size, and the seeds of an instance are averaged into one observation. The procedure stops
at the first instance that triggers a declaration and refuses data after it, because the
pre-registered protocol ends there; a warning lists what was not consumed (here, the instances
after the declaration). `comparison_report()` (also `summary()`) returns the result contract,
`tidy()` the trajectory (one row per instance with the interval, its running intersection, the
cost and the decision at that time), `glance()` a one-row summary, and `autoplot()` the
confidence sequence against the number of instances with the equivalence band
(Figure \@ref(fig:fig-workflow)).

```{r fig-workflow, echo = TRUE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.2, out.width = "100%", fig.cap = "Output of autoplot() for the comparison above: running confidence sequence for the mean paired difference (ribbon), estimate (line) and equivalence band [-0.02, 0.02] (grey). The procedure stops when the whole ribbon is above the band.", fig.alt = "A shaded band that narrows as instances accumulate and ends entirely above the grey equivalence band."}
ggplot2::autoplot(state)
```

## The result contract

Every comparison reports the estimand (as a sentence), the estimate, the current confidence
sequence, the boundary and its validity flag, the assumptions in words (four, or five with a
declared variance bound), the decision and stopping reason, diagnostics (instances,
evaluations, losses at the bounds, an empty-set flag), the resources consumed against the
budget, the instance and seed identifiers in the order observed, and the package and R
versions. The intent is that a reader can audit a decision without rerunning it.

## Refusals

The package never converts invalid input into a valid-looking result. A loss outside the
declared bounds is an error, not a clipped value; a missing loss is an error, not a dropped
row; a negative or infinite cost is an error; a duplicated (instance, seed) pair is an error;
an instance that reappears after its losses were observed is an error whose message explains
(A4); `paired = FALSE` is an error stating that unpaired designs are not implemented; and
updating after a terminal decision is an error too.

## Implementation notes {#sec-implementation}

Each boundary is a small state machine with sufficient statistics, exposed through three
kernels that other packages can reuse: `boundary_init()` creates the state, `boundary_update()`
absorbs one observation and `boundary_interval()` reads the current confidence set. The betting
boundary keeps the hedged log-capital on a grid of candidate means (1,001 points by default);
its confidence set is the set of means at which the capital is below $1/\alpha$, which
@waudbysmith2024 show to be an interval. The package reports the outer edges of the grid cells
that contain the endpoints, so that the reported set contains the exact one, and refines both
endpoints on the exact capital once per call of `update_comparison()`; a nonempty set narrower
than one grid cell is located by minimising the exact capital rather than reported as empty.

Decisions do not depend on the grid. Because the confidence sets are intervals, each rule of
the decision rule in [Section 3](#sec-protocol) is equivalent to a statement about the two thresholds: B is declared
when $+\delta$ has left the running set and the set lies above it, and so on. The package
therefore tracks the exact capital at the two thresholds, which costs $O(1)$ per instance, and
records on which side of a threshold the set lies when the capital excludes it; every later
set is contained in that one, so the side never changes. The per-instance cost is linear in
the grid size and does not grow with the length of the stream. A stream of 8,000 instances
exactly at the margin, which never decides, takes about 6 s on a 2015-era desktop processor
(Intel Core i5-6500, R 4.6.1).

# Simulation study {#sec-sim}

## Design

The study was frozen before results were available: configuration files are dated and never
edited, and changes are new files. Its analysis script was written and tested on a
three-replication smoke run before the study ran. All code is in the `experiments/` directory
of the package repository.^[<https://github.com/castlaboratory/seqbench>, outside the R
package sources.] Losses are generated as $L_A = u_i + \eta_{is}$ and
$L_B = u_i' + \eta'_{is} - \mu + e_{is}$, with an instance effect $u_i \sim U(0.45, 0.70)$
shared by both algorithms when paired ($u_i' = u_i$) and drawn independently otherwise, seed
noise $\eta, \eta' \sim U(-h_{seed}, h_{seed})$ and comparison noise $e \sim U(-h, h)$; then
$E[L_A - L_B] = \mu$ exactly, all losses lie in $[0.047, 0.903] \subset [0, 1]$, and the
standard deviation of the per-instance difference is known. The baseline grid crosses
$\mu \in \{0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20\}$ (null, true equivalence, exactly at the margin,
moderate, large and very large effects) with $\text{sd}(D) \in \{0.03, 0.10\}$, with
$\alpha = 0.05$, $\delta = 0.02$, bounds $[0, 1]$ and a budget of 2,000 instances. Two
ablations use the high noise level: unpaired instances, and five seeds per instance with seed
noise $h_{seed} = 0.03$. Each of the 24 cells has 2,000 replications, and every method sees the
same simulated stream in a given replication (seeded by cell and replication only), so method
comparisons are paired.

Two amendments, frozen on 2026-09-26 after an external review and run with the same methods
and replication count, add 14 cells with negative effects and with effects 0.005 and 0.01 away
from a threshold ($\mu \in \{-0.20, -0.05, -0.025, -0.015, 0.015, 0.025, 0.03\}$, both noise
levels), and 12 seed-cluster cells with an instance-specific differential effect
(see "Pairing and seed clusters" below). One amended cell ($\mu = -0.20$, high noise) is invalid by
construction: its losses for B reach 1.07, and the package refused every replication rather
than clip. It is reported as such and excluded; the other 13 cells cover the negative
direction.

Eight procedures are compared: the three distribution-free boundaries and the invalid
control; fixed-sample $t$ intervals at $n = 100$, $500$ and $2{,}000$ instances with the same
three-way margin rule and no adaptation; and the anytime-valid confidence sequence of the
sequential $t$-test of \pkg{safestats} [`saviTTest()`, @safestats; @ly2024] with the same
running intersection and margin rule. Its design is fixed before the stream with the *true*
standard deviation of the data-generating process, an oracle that favours \pkg{safestats},
which assumes Gaussian data while ours are sums of uniforms.

The metrics are false declarations (a declaration that contradicts the truth; at
$\mu = \delta$ the truth is "equivalent"), coverage failure (the true mean leaves the reported
running intersection at some time up to stopping), the proportion of inconclusive outcomes,
and the number of instances consumed. Rates carry Wilson intervals, medians percentile
bootstrap intervals over replications, and ratios of medians paired bootstrap intervals. With
2,000 replications the Monte Carlo standard error of a rate near 0.05 is 0.005, and zero
observed events give an upper Wilson bound of 0.0019.

## Validity

Table \@ref(tab:tab2) gives, for each procedure, the largest false-declaration rate and the
largest coverage-failure rate over the 24 cells.

```{r tab2}
lab <- c("seqbench:betting" = "betting", "seqbench:empirical_bernstein" = "empirical Bernstein",
         "seqbench:hoeffding" = "Hoeffding", "fixed:100" = "fixed $n = 100$",
         "fixed:500" = "fixed $n = 500$", "fixed:final" = "fixed $n = 2000$",
         "savi_cs" = "\\pkg{safestats} CS, oracle sd", "seqbench:naive_fixed" = "naive fixed (invalid)")
abl <- c(none = "", unpaired = ", unpaired", cluster = ", five seeds")
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(lab), function(m) {
  d <- t1[t1$method == m, ]; i <- which.max(d$false_rate)
  where <- if (d$false_rate[i] > 0) sprintf(" ($\\mu = %s$%s)", d$mu[i], abl[[d$ablation[i]]]) else ""
  data.frame(Procedure = lab[[m]],
             fd = sprintf("%.4f%s [%.4f, %.4f]", d$false_rate[i], where, d$false_lo[i], d$false_hi[i]),
             cov = sprintf("%.4f", max(d$miscover_rate)))
}))
names(tab) <- c("Procedure", "max false declaration [95\\% Wilson]", "max coverage failure")
knitr::kable(tab, caption = "Maximum rates over the 24 cells (2,000 replications each), with the cell of the maximum false-declaration rate and its 95\\% Wilson interval.",
             escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 8)
```

The three distribution-free boundaries stay far inside their nominal level. Their few false
declarations are concentrated at the exact margin, where "equivalent" is the only correct
answer and a superiority declaration is a legitimate $\alpha$-event. The fixed-sample tests and
the Gaussian sequence sit near their nominal level. The repeatedly inspected $t$-test issues a
false declaration in `r pct(nf$false_rate[nf$mu == 0.02], 0)` of the runs at the margin,
`r pct(nf$false_rate[nf$mu == 0.01], 0)` under true equivalence and
`r pct(nf$false_rate[nf$mu == 0], 0)` under the null, and its interval misses the truth at
some inspection in up to `r pct(mx("seqbench:naive_fixed", "miscover_rate"), 0)` of the runs:
this is the behaviour of a benchmark that peeks. In
`r sum(t1$method == "seqbench:naive_fixed" & t1$exceeds_alpha)` of its 24 cells the lower
Wilson bound of the false-declaration rate is above $\alpha$.

## Cost

```{r tab3}
d <- base[base$h > 0.1, ]
cell <- function(m, p) ifelse(p >= 0.9, "budget", ifelse(p > 0.005, sprintf("%.0f$^{%.0f\\%%}$", m, 100 * p), sprintf("%.0f", m)))
w <- reshape(data.frame(method = d$method, mu = d$mu, v = cell(d$median_n, d$p_inconclusive)),
             idvar = "method", timevar = "mu", direction = "wide")
w <- w[match(names(lab), w$method), ]
w$method <- lab[w$method]
names(w) <- c("Procedure", paste0("$\\mu = ", sort(unique(d$mu)), "$"))
dd <- d[!d$method %in% c("seqbench:naive_fixed", "seqbench:hoeffding") & !grepl("^fixed", d$method) & d$p_inconclusive < 0.9, ]
relw <- max(pmax(dd$median_hi / dd$median_n - 1, 1 - dd$median_lo / dd$median_n))
knitr::kable(w, caption = paste0("Median instances to stopping, baseline cells with $\\text{sd}(D) = 0.10$, 2,000 replications. A superscript gives the percentage of inconclusive runs when above 0.5\\%; ``budget'' marks cells where at least 90\\% of the runs exhausted the 2,000 instances. For the valid sequential procedures the bootstrap 95\\% intervals of the medians are within ", round(100 * relw), "\\% of the reported value."),
             escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", rep("r", 6))) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 8)
```

```{r cost-numbers}
g <- function(m, mu, h = 0.173, col = "median_n") base[base$method == m & base$mu == mu & abs(base$h - h) < 1e-6, col]
eb_ratio <- base$ratio_to_betting[base$method == "seqbench:empirical_bernstein" & base$p_inconclusive < 0.5 & base$mu != 0.02]
sv_hi <- sv[sv$h > 0.1, ]; sv_lo <- sv[sv$h < 0.1, ]
```

Three readings. First, adaptation pays. The betting sequence resolves the null in a median of
`r num(g("seqbench:betting", 0))` instances and the moderate effect in
`r num(g("seqbench:betting", 0.05))`, whereas a fixed sample of 100 is inconclusive in
`r pct(g("fixed:100", 0, col = "p_inconclusive"), 0)` of the runs under the null and a fixed
sample of 500 in `r pct(g("fixed:500", 0.01, col = "p_inconclusive"), 0)` at $\mu = 0.01$.
Second, the distribution-free boundaries are ordered as expected: empirical Bernstein needs
`r sprintf("%.1f", min(eb_ratio))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(eb_ratio))` times the instances of
betting, and Hoeffding resolves only the very large effect within the budget. Third, and this is
the number a benchmarker should see before choosing, the Gaussian sequence with a known variance
needs `r sprintf("%.2f", min(sv_hi$ratio_to_betting))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(sv_hi$ratio_to_betting))`
of the instances of the betting sequence at this noise level and
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(sv_lo$ratio_to_betting))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(sv_lo$ratio_to_betting))`
at the low noise level (Table \@ref(tab:tab4)), that is, `r sprintf("%.1f", 1 / max(sv$ratio_to_betting))`
to `r sprintf("%.0f", 1 / min(sv$ratio_to_betting))` times fewer. The truncated-bet analysis below
explains the mechanism, and [Section 8](#sec-limitations) draws the consequence.

```{r tab4}
r <- sv[order(sv$h, sv$mu), ]
w <- data.frame(sd = ifelse(r$h < 0.1, "0.03", "0.10"), mu = r$mu,
                v = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f--%.3f)", r$ratio_to_betting, r$ratio_lo, r$ratio_hi))
w <- reshape(w, idvar = "sd", timevar = "mu", direction = "wide")
names(w) <- c("$\\text{sd}(D)$", paste0("$\\mu = ", sort(unique(r$mu)), "$"))
knitr::kable(w, caption = "Ratio of median instances, \\pkg{safestats} CS over betting, with the paired bootstrap 95\\% interval, baseline cells.",
             escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", rep("r", 5))) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "scale_down"))
```

## Pairing and seed clusters {#sec-clusters}

```{r tab5}
t3$lab <- ifelse(t3$ablation == "unpaired", "unpaired", "five seeds")
t3o <- t3[t3$mu != 0.02, ]
w <- rbind(
  data.frame(a = paste(t3o$lab, "instances", sep = ", "), mu = t3o$mu, v = sprintf("%.2f", t3o$ratio_n)),
  data.frame(a = paste(t3o$lab, "evaluations", sep = ", "), mu = t3o$mu, v = sprintf("%.2f", t3o$ratio_cost)))
w <- reshape(w, idvar = "a", timevar = "mu", direction = "wide")
w <- w[order(match(w$a, c("unpaired, instances", "unpaired, evaluations", "five seeds, instances", "five seeds, evaluations"))), ]
names(w) <- c("Ablation", paste0("$\\mu = ", sort(unique(t3o$mu)), "$"))
knitr::kable(w, caption = "Betting boundary, $\\text{sd}(D) = 0.10$: ratio of median instances and of mean evaluations (both algorithms, all seeds) relative to the paired single-seed design.",
             escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 8)
```

Pairing by instance costs nothing and saves up to `r pct(1 - 1 / max(t3o$ratio_n[t3o$ablation == "unpaired"]), 0)`
of the instances in the hard cells: at $\mu = 0.01$ it turns
`r pct(t3$p_inconclusive[t3$ablation == "unpaired" & t3$mu == 0.01], 0)` inconclusive runs into
`r pct(t3$p_inc_paired[t3$ablation == "unpaired" & t3$mu == 0.01], 0)`. Averaging five seeds
per instance saves up to `r pct(1 - min(t3o$ratio_n[t3o$ablation == "cluster"]), 0)` of the
*instances* but costs `r sprintf("%.1f", min(t3o$ratio_cost[t3o$ablation == "cluster"]))` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", max(t3o$ratio_cost[t3o$ablation == "cluster"]))` times the *evaluations*. In
this design the instance effect cancels exactly under pairing, so seed averaging only reduces
independent seed noise, and its benefit is confined to the cells where the variance matters at
all (see the truncated-bet analysis below).

```{r cluster-numbers}
c8 <- t8[t8$w > 0, ]
icc8 <- (0.05^2 / 3) / (0.05^2 / 3 + (0.173^2 + 2 * 0.03^2) / 3)
pr5 <- c8[c8$method == "pseudorep:betting" & c8$seeds == 5, ]
co5 <- c8[c8$method == "seqbench:betting" & c8$seeds == 5, ]
```

The cluster amendment adds to the paired difference an instance-specific term
$v_i \sim U(-w, w)$ shared by all seeds of instance $i$, so that the differences within an
instance are positively correlated and an analysis by row is genuinely invalid. With $w = 0.05$
the intra-instance correlation is `r sprintf("%.2f", icc8)` and the design effect of five seeds
is `r sprintf("%.1f", 1 + 4 * icc8)`. Table \@ref(tab:tab7) compares the correct analysis (one
sequential unit per instance) with pseudoreplication (every (instance, seed) row fed as its own
instance).

```{r tab7}
t8w <- t8[t8$w > 0 & !(t8$method == "pseudorep:betting" & t8$seeds == 1L), ]   # one-seed pseudoreplication is the one-seed analysis
lab8 <- c("seqbench:betting" = "betting", "pseudorep:betting" = "betting, pseudoreplication",
          "seqbench:empirical_bernstein" = "empirical Bernstein", "fixed:final" = "fixed $n = 2000$")
t8w$inst <- ifelse(t8w$method == "pseudorep:betting", t8w$median_n / t8w$seeds, t8w$median_n)
cell8 <- function(n, ev, p) paste0(sprintf("%.0f", n), ifelse(p > 0.005, sprintf("$^{%.0f\\%%}$", 100 * p), ""), " (", sprintf("%.0f", ev), ")")
t8w$v <- cell8(t8w$inst, t8w$mean_cost, t8w$p_inconclusive)
w <- reshape(t8w[, c("method", "seeds", "mu", "v")], idvar = c("method", "seeds"), timevar = "mu", direction = "wide")
mc <- aggregate(miscover_rate ~ method + seeds, t8w, max); names(mc)[3] <- "cov"
w <- merge(w, mc)
w <- w[order(match(w$method, names(lab8)), w$seeds), ]
w$method <- lab8[w$method]
w$cov <- sprintf("%.2f\\%%", 100 * w$cov)
names(w) <- c("Procedure", "Seeds", paste0("$\\mu = ", sort(unique(t8w$mu)), "$"), "Max. cov. failure")
knitr::kable(w, caption = "Seed clusters with an instance-specific differential effect ($w = 0.05$), 2,000 replications: median instances to stopping (mean evaluations of both algorithms in parentheses; a superscript gives the percentage of inconclusive runs when above 0.5\\%) and the largest coverage-failure rate over the three effect sizes. For pseudoreplication the instances are the rows divided by five.",
             escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "c", rep("r", 4))) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "scale_down"))
```

The result is negative, and we report it as measured. Pseudoreplication produced
`r sum(c8$false_declaration[c8$method == "pseudorep:betting"])` false declarations in
`r num(sum(c8$R[c8$method == "pseudorep:betting"]))` runs, and its coverage failure rose only to
`r pct(max(pr5$miscover_rate))` with five seeds, against `r pct(max(co5$miscover_rate), 2)` for
the correct analysis: a design effect of 1.3 is absorbed by the slack of the betting boundary
documented in the coverage audit below. Its cost equals that of a single-seed analysis because
it consumes the same rows under another label. The correct five-seed analysis saves
`r pct(1 - max(co5$ratio_n_vs_1seed), 0)` to `r pct(1 - min(co5$ratio_n_vs_1seed), 0)` of the
*instances* against one seed and costs `r sprintf("%.1f", min(co5$ratio_cost_vs_1seed))` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", max(co5$ratio_cost_vs_1seed))` times the *evaluations*, as in the first
ablation. The conclusion for practice is unchanged. Seeds are a cluster, not replications,
and averaging them is worth its price only when instances are expensive relative to
evaluations. The guarantee did not visibly break here because the correlation was mild, not
because pseudoreplication is safe; the vaccination application of [Section 6](#sec-apps)
measures a strong correlation.

## Why the cost is what it is: the truncated-bet regime {#sec-regime}

The betting sequence bets a predictable fraction
$\tilde\lambda_t = \sqrt{2\log(2/\alpha)/(\hat\sigma^2_{t-1}\, t \log(t+1))}$, truncated at
$c/m$ and $c/(1-m)$ for the candidate mean $m$; with $c = 1/2$ the cap is close to 1 near
$m = 1/2$. While $\tilde\lambda_t$ exceeds the cap, that is, while
$t\log(t+1) < 2\log(2/\alpha)/(\hat\sigma^2 \cdot \text{cap}^2)$, the bet is constant, and for
small variance the log-capital at a candidate at distance $g$ from $\nu$ grows by about
$\text{cap} \cdot g$ per instance. With the hedging weight $1/2$, a threshold is excluded once
that log-capital reaches $\log(2/\alpha)$, so the stopping time is approximately

$$\tau \approx \frac{\log(2/\alpha)}{\text{cap}\cdot g} = \frac{\log(2/\alpha)\,(b-a)}{\text{cap}\cdot\big|\,|\mu| - \delta\,\big|},$$

linear in the inverse distance to the nearest threshold and *independent of the variance*.
Table \@ref(tab:tab6) compares this prediction with the observed medians.

```{r tab6}
b4 <- t4[t4$method == "seqbench:betting", ]
lo4 <- b4[b4$h < 0.1, ]; hi4 <- b4[b4$h > 0.1, ]
w <- data.frame(mu = sprintf("%.2f", lo4$mu), dist = sprintf("%.2f", lo4$distance),
                obs_lo = sprintf("%.0f", lo4$median_n), pred = sprintf("%.0f", lo4$pred_truncated),
                obs_hi = sprintf("%.0f", hi4$median_n[match(lo4$mu, hi4$mu)]))
names(w) <- c("$\\mu$", "distance", "observed, sd 0.03", "predicted", "observed, sd 0.10")
knitr::kable(w, caption = sprintf("Betting boundary: median instances observed and predicted by the truncated-bet approximation, for $\\text{sd}(D) = 0.03$ (crossover at $t \\approx %s$) and $0.10$ (crossover at $t \\approx %s$).", num(lo4$crossover_t[1]), num(hi4$crossover_t[1])),
             escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 8)
fit <- lm(log(median_n) ~ method + log(distance) + log(sd_d), data = t4[t4$p_inconclusive < 0.5, ])
cf <- summary(fit)$coefficients
```

At the low noise level the prediction is within `r pct(max(abs(lo4$ratio_obs_pred - 1)), 0)` of
the observed median everywhere. At the high noise level it holds where the decision comes
before the crossover and degrades to `r sprintf("%.2f", min(hi4$ratio_obs_pred[hi4$median_n > hi4$crossover_t]))`--`r sprintf("%.2f", max(hi4$ratio_obs_pred[hi4$median_n > hi4$crossover_t]))`
times the prediction where it comes after, when the variance term of the bet becomes active.
Figure \@ref(fig:regimes) shows the observed medians against the prediction. A log-log
regression of the median stopping time on the distance and the standard deviation over the
resolved cells of both boundaries, with a boundary-specific intercept, gives slopes
`r sprintf("%.2f", cf["log(distance)", 1])` (s.e. `r sprintf("%.2f", cf["log(distance)", 2])`)
and `r sprintf("%+.2f", cf["log(sd_d)", 1])` (`r sprintf("%.2f", cf["log(sd_d)", 2])`).

```{r regimes, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%", fig.cap = "Median instances to decision against the distance to the nearest decision threshold (log-log), betting and empirical-Bernstein boundaries, two noise levels, 2,000 replications per point. Lines: the truncated-bet prediction.", fig.alt = "Log-log scatter of median stopping time versus distance with two straight prediction lines; points fall on the lines except at the smallest distances for the higher noise level."}
f2 <- t4
f2$boundary <- ifelse(f2$method == "seqbench:betting", "betting", "empirical Bernstein")
ggplot(f2, aes(distance, median_n, colour = boundary)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pred_truncated, linetype = "truncated-bet prediction")) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = factor(round(sd_d, 2))), size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "distance to the nearest threshold, ||mu| - delta| (loss units)",
       y = "median instances to decision", colour = "boundary", shape = "sd(D)", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

There are two practical consequences. In low-noise benchmarks with a tight margin, halving
the distance to the threshold doubles the cost rather than quadrupling it. And the boundary
cannot exploit a small variance beyond its bet cap, which is why the Gaussian sequence, whose
bet scales with $g/\sigma^2$, is so much faster when $\sigma$ is small. Raising the cap helps at
a small, measurable price. In a sweep on the twelve baseline cells (2,000 replications each,
same streams), $c = 0.9$ needed 222 instead of 388 instances at the null and 143 instead of 254
at $\mu = 0.05$ for $\text{sd}(D) = 0.03$ (385 and 165 instead of 496 and 272 at
$\text{sd}(D) = 0.10$), while the largest false-declaration rate rose from 0.20% to 0.70% and
the largest coverage failure from 0.55% to 1.40%, both still far below $\alpha$; $c = 0.99$
gained little more. Coverage is guaranteed for any $c \in (0, 1)$.

## Time-uniform coverage without stopping {#sec-audit}

Coverage in Table \@ref(tab:tab2) is measured up to the stopping time. A separate audit ran
each boundary over the full stream of 2,000 instances in the same 24 cells (same seeds, hence
the same streams; for the betting boundary the exact capital at the true mean is evaluated,
which needs no grid) and recorded whether the true mean ever left the running confidence
sequence. Over 2,000 replications per cell the largest failure rate was 1.55% for betting,
0.25% for empirical Bernstein and 0 for Hoeffding, against the nominal 5%. The time-uniform
guarantee holds with room to spare, which is the other face of the cost measured above.

## Negative effects and effects near the margin {#sec-extra}

```{r extra-numbers}
v7 <- t7[grepl("^seqbench:(betting|empirical|hoeff)", t7$method), ]
e <- function(m, mu, h, col) t7[t7$method == m & abs(t7$mu - mu) < 1e-9 & abs(t7$h - h) < 1e-6, col]
near_hi <- t7[abs(abs(t7$mu) - 0.02) < 0.0051 & t7$h > 0.1, ]
near_lo <- t7[abs(abs(t7$mu) - 0.02) < 0.0051 & t7$h < 0.1, ]
ph <- function(s) planning_horizon(comparison_design(margin = 0.02, bounds = c(0, 1)), 0.005, sd = s)
```

The first amendment fills two gaps of the baseline grid: effects in the direction of A, and
effects 0.005 and 0.01 away from a decision threshold ($|\mu| \in \{0.015, 0.025, 0.03\}$ with
$\delta = 0.02$). Over its 13 valid cells no distribution-free boundary made a false
declaration (`r sum(v7$false_declaration)` in `r num(sum(v7$R))` runs; upper Wilson bound 0.19% per
cell), whereas the \pkg{safestats} sequence reached `r pct(max(t7$false_rate[t7$method == "savi_cs"]), 2)`
and the repeatedly inspected $t$-test `r pct(max(t7$false_rate[t7$method == "seqbench:naive_fixed"]))`.
Coverage failure up to stopping was at most `r pct(max(t7$miscover_rate[t7$method == "seqbench:betting"]), 2)`
for betting and 0 for the other two boundaries. Table \@ref(tab:tab8) gives the cost.

```{r tab8}
lab7 <- c("seqbench:betting" = "betting", "seqbench:empirical_bernstein" = "empirical Bernstein",
          "seqbench:hoeffding" = "Hoeffding", "fixed:500" = "fixed $n = 500$",
          "savi_cs" = "\\pkg{safestats} CS, oracle sd")
t7s <- t7[t7$method %in% names(lab7), ]
t7s$v <- cell(t7s$median_n, t7s$p_inconclusive)
mus <- sort(unique(t7s$mu))
w <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sort(unique(t7s$h)), function(hh) do.call(rbind, lapply(names(lab7), function(m) {
  x <- t7s[t7s$h == hh & t7s$method == m, ]
  data.frame(sd = ifelse(hh < 0.1, "0.03", "0.10"), method = lab7[[m]],
             t(ifelse(is.na(match(mus, x$mu)), "---", x$v[match(mus, x$mu)])))
}))))
w$sd[duplicated(w$sd)] <- ""
names(w) <- c("$\\text{sd}(D)$", "Procedure", paste0("$", mus, "$"))
knitr::kable(w, caption = "Median instances to stopping in the amended cells ($\\mu$ in the column heads; $\\delta = 0.02$), 2,000 replications, same conventions as Table 3; ``---'' marks the cell that is invalid by construction.",
             escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "l", rep("r", 7))) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "scale_down"))
```

Two readings. The procedures are symmetric in the sign of $\mu$, as they should be: the betting
boundary needs `r num(e("seqbench:betting", -0.05, 0.052, "median_n"))` and
`r num(e("seqbench:betting", -0.05, 0.173, "median_n"))` instances at $\mu = -0.05$ against
`r num(g("seqbench:betting", 0.05, 0.052))` and `r num(g("seqbench:betting", 0.05))` at $+0.05$.
And a distance of 0.005 from a threshold is beyond every procedure at the high noise level, the
Gaussian oracle included: \pkg{safestats} is inconclusive in
`r pct(min(near_hi$p_inconclusive[near_hi$method == "savi_cs"]), 0)`--`r pct(max(near_hi$p_inconclusive[near_hi$method == "savi_cs"]), 0)`
of the runs and betting in `r pct(min(near_hi$p_inconclusive[near_hi$method == "seqbench:betting"]), 0)`--`r pct(max(near_hi$p_inconclusive[near_hi$method == "seqbench:betting"]), 0)`.
At the low noise level betting resolves these cells in a median of about
`r num(100 * round(mean(near_lo$median_n[near_lo$method == "seqbench:betting"]) / 100))` instances with
`r pct(min(near_lo$p_inconclusive[near_lo$method == "seqbench:betting"]), 0)` to
`r pct(max(near_lo$p_inconclusive[near_lo$method == "seqbench:betting"]), 0)` inconclusive runs, and
the Gaussian sequence in about `r num(100 * round(mean(near_lo$median_n[near_lo$method == "savi_cs"]) / 100))`.
Before the first instance is run, `planning_horizon()` with the true standard deviation returns
`r num(ph(0.03))` (low noise) and `r num(ph(0.10))` (high noise) instances for this distance,
both beyond the budget of 2,000: this is where a benchmarker should learn that a distance of
0.005 is not a question the budget can answer.

# Applications {#sec-apps}

The first two applications were frozen on 2026-10-23, before any loss was computed. Each
defines a population of instances by a random generator. To measure operating
characteristics with a known truth, a pool of 10,000 i.i.d. instances is generated once and
1,000 streams are resampled from it with replacement. The resampling population is the pool's
empirical distribution, whose mean is known exactly, so false declarations and coverage can be
counted; for the generator population itself the pool mean is an estimate, with a Monte Carlo
standard error of `r sprintf("%.4f", pool("cvrp")$sd / 100)` (routing) and
`r sprintf("%.4f", pool("epidemic", 5L)$sd / 100)` (vaccination). The pool in generation order is also a live
stream of fresh instances, which is how a user would run the comparison
(Figure \@ref(fig:fig-apps)). The procedures are the betting and empirical-Bernstein
boundaries, fixed samples of 100 and 3,000 instances, and the \pkg{safestats} sequence, whose
design now uses the standard deviation of an independent pilot of 200 instances, as a user
would; the vaccination study adds the invalid pseudoreplication analysis.

```{r apps-numbers}
cv <- pool("cvrp"); ep5 <- pool("epidemic", 5L); ep1 <- pool("epidemic", 1L)
cvb <- app("cvrp", "seqbench:betting"); cve <- app("cvrp", "seqbench:empirical_bernstein")
cvs <- app("cvrp", "savi_cs"); cvf <- app("cvrp", "fixed:100"); cvF <- app("cvrp", "fixed:final")
eb5 <- app("epidemic", "seqbench:betting", 5L); eb1 <- app("epidemic", "seqbench:betting", 1L)
ee5 <- app("epidemic", "seqbench:empirical_bernstein", 5L)
es5 <- app("epidemic", "savi_cs", 5L); es1 <- app("epidemic", "savi_cs", 1L)
ep5r <- app("epidemic", "pseudorep:betting", 5L)
dec_word <- function(x) switch(x, A = "A is relevantly better", B = "B is relevantly better",
                               equivalent = "practically equivalent", x)
```

## Vehicle routing heuristics {#sec-cvrp}

A distribution planner must choose a constructive heuristic for the capacitated vehicle
routing problem [@toth2014]: the sweep algorithm of @gillett1974 (A) or the savings algorithm
of @clarke1964 (B), both followed by 2-opt inside each route [@croes1958]. Instances follow the
generator logic of @uchoa2017: 50 to 150 customers in the unit square, a central, eccentric or
random depot, uniform, clustered or mixed customer positions, unitary, small or large demands,
and a capacity giving 4 to 25 customers per route on average. The loss is the relative gap
$1 - LB/z$ of the solution cost $z$ to the lower bound
$LB = \max\{\text{MST},\ 2\sum_i q_i d_{0i}/Q\}$, the larger of the minimum spanning tree of the
depot and customers and the radial bound. It lies in $[0, 1)$ for any feasible solution by
construction, so the bounds $[0, 1]$ need no truncation. The margin is one percentage point of
gap ($\delta = 0.01$) and the cost is CPU time. The pool mean is
$\mu = `r sprintf("%.4f", cv$mu)`$ (sd `r sprintf("%.3f", cv$sd)`, skewness
`r sprintf("%.2f", cv$skewness)`): the savings algorithm closes about
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * cv$mu)` percentage points more of the gap.

On the live stream the betting sequence declared "`r dec_word(live("cvrp")$decision)`" after
`r num(live("cvrp")$n_instances)` instances (`r sprintf("%.1f", live("cvrp")$cpu_seconds)` CPU
seconds), with final interval $[`r sprintf("%.3f", live("cvrp")$lower)`, `r sprintf("%.3f", live("cvrp")$upper)`]$;
empirical Bernstein needed `r num(live("cvrp", "empirical_bernstein")$n_instances)`. Over 1,000
resampled streams every procedure declared B in `r pct(min(a10$p_B[a10$app == "cvrp"]), 0)` of
the runs, with no false declaration. The effect is large relative to the margin, so a fixed
sample of 100 instances would also have sufficed; the sequential procedures find this out
without knowing it in advance, while a cautious fixed sample of 3,000 instances spends
`r num(cvF$mean_cost, 0)` CPU seconds against `r num(cvb$mean_cost, 1)` for the betting
sequence (median `r num(cvb$median_n)` instances; empirical Bernstein `r num(cve$median_n)`,
the pilot-designed Gaussian sequence `r num(cvs$median_n)`). Coverage failure up to stopping was
`r pct(cvb$miscover_rate)` for betting, `r pct(cvs$miscover_rate)` for the Gaussian sequence
and `r pct(cvf$miscover_rate)` for the fixed sample of 100, which has a single, nominal 95%
interval. Table \@ref(tab:tab-apps) collects the results of both applications.

## Vaccination strategies on contact networks {#sec-epidemic}

With the same number of doses, does vaccinating the highest-degree people (degree targeting,
B), which needs the full contact network, reduce the final attack rate of an epidemic by a
practically relevant amount relative to acquaintance immunisation [@cohen2003], which
vaccinates a random contact of a random person and needs only local information (A)? Both
improve on random vaccination in heterogeneous networks [@pastorsatorras2002]. Instances are
networks of 1,000 to 3,000 people drawn from five models (Erdős--Rényi, Barabási--Albert, Watts--Strogatz,
stochastic block model with 5 to 20 communities, and power-law Chung--Lu), with
$R_0 \sim U(1.5, 3)$, vaccine coverage between 5% and 20%, and five index cases. The
epidemic is an SIR process with a fixed infectious period; its final size is exactly the size
of the union of the index cases' clusters in bond percolation on the network without the
vaccinated [@newman2002; @kenah2007], which is how it is simulated with \CRANpkg{igraph}
[@igraph]. The loss is the attack rate, the fraction of the population infected, in $[0, 1]$ by
construction, and the margin is one percentage point ($\delta = 0.01$). Each instance has five
seeds, independent epidemics in which both strategies share the percolated network and the
order from which index cases are taken (common random numbers), so the pairing is by
(instance, seed) and the seeds of a network form a cluster.

The pool is not Gaussian: the per-network difference has skewness
`r sprintf("%.2f", ep1$skewness)` with one seed and `r pct(ep1$ties, 1)` exact ties (both
strategies stop the epidemic, or both fail to), and the differences of the five simulations of
a network are strongly correlated, with an intra-network correlation of
`r sprintf("%.2f", ep5$icc)` and a design effect of `r sprintf("%.1f", ep5$design_effect)`.
Degree targeting lowers the attack rate by $\mu = `r sprintf("%.3f", ep5$mu)`$ on average,
far beyond the margin. On the live stream the five-seed betting analysis declared
"`r dec_word(live("epidemic", s = 5L)$decision)`" after `r num(live("epidemic", s = 5L)$n_instances)`
networks (`r num(live("epidemic", s = 5L)$n_evaluations)` paired simulations). Over the
resampled streams every procedure declared B in every run. The informative comparison is the
cost of the two designs: the five-seed analysis needed a median of `r num(eb5$median_n)`
networks and the one-seed analysis `r num(eb1$median_n)`, at `r num(eb5$mean_cost, 1)` against
`r num(eb1$mean_cost, 1)` CPU seconds. Averaging five epidemics per network bought nothing,
because the betting sequence decides here in its truncated-bet regime, where the stopping time
does not depend on the variance ([Section 5](#sec-sim), truncated-bet regime); one simulation per network, and
more networks, is the better design. The invalid pseudoreplication analysis stopped after a
median of `r num(ep5r$median_n)` simulations, about `r num(ep5r$median_n / 5)` networks, and its
interval missed the truth in `r pct(ep5r$miscover_rate)` of the streams against
`r pct(eb5$miscover_rate)` for the correct analysis. With an effect `r sprintf("%.0f", ep5$mu / 0.01)`
times the margin this did not produce false declarations, but its interval treats correlated
simulations as independent evidence, and no guarantee covers it. The pilot-designed Gaussian
sequence did not lose coverage on these data.

```{r tab-apps}
labA <- c("seqbench:betting" = "betting", "seqbench:empirical_bernstein" = "empirical Bernstein",
          "fixed:100" = "fixed $n = 100$", "fixed:final" = "fixed $n = 3000$",
          "savi_cs" = "\\pkg{safestats} CS, pilot sd", "pseudorep:betting" = "betting, pseudoreplication (invalid)")
x <- a10[a10$method %in% names(labA) & !(a10$method == "pseudorep:betting" & a10$seeds == 1L), ]   # one-seed pseudoreplication is the one-seed analysis
x <- x[order(match(x$app, c("cvrp", "epidemic")), -x$seeds, match(x$method, names(labA))), ]
w <- data.frame(Application = ifelse(x$app == "cvrp", "routing", paste0("epidemic, ", x$seeds, " seed", ifelse(x$seeds > 1, "s", ""))),
                Procedure = labA[x$method],
                Declared = sprintf("%.1f\\%%", 100 * ifelse(x$truth == "A", x$p_A, ifelse(x$truth == "B", x$p_B, x$p_equivalent))),
                False = sprintf("%.1f\\%%", 100 * x$false_rate),
                Inconclusive = sprintf("%.1f\\%%", 100 * x$p_inconclusive),
                Coverage = sprintf("%.1f\\%%", 100 * x$miscover_rate),
                Median = sprintf("%.0f", x$median_n), CPU = sprintf("%.1f", x$mean_cost))
w$Application[duplicated(w$Application)] <- ""
names(w) <- c("Application", "Procedure", "correct", "false", "inconcl.", "cov. failure", "median $n$", "CPU s")
knitr::kable(w, caption = "Applications, 1,000 streams resampled from each frozen pool: rates of correct declarations, false declarations and inconclusive outcomes, coverage failure up to stopping, median instances to stopping and mean CPU seconds consumed. For pseudoreplication the median counts simulations, not networks.",
             escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", align = c("l", "l", rep("r", 6))) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "scale_down"))
```

```{r fig-apps, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3, out.width = "100%", fig.cap = "Live runs of the betting sequence on fresh instances in generation order: running confidence sequence for the mean paired difference against the number of instances (networks, for the epidemic with five seeds each), with the equivalence band. Left: acquaintance minus degree targeting, attack rate. Right: sweep minus savings, relative gap. The vertical axis is cut at [-0.1, 0.3]; the early intervals are wider.", fig.alt = "Two panels, each with a shaded band narrowing over instances until it lies entirely above the grey equivalence band."}
f3$panel <- ifelse(f3$app == "cvrp", "vehicle routing", paste0("vaccination (", f3$seeds, " seeds)"))
f3 <- f3[f3$app == "cvrp" | f3$seeds == 5, ]
ggplot(f3, aes(t)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -0.01, ymax = 0.01, alpha = 0.15, fill = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower_running, ymax = upper_running), alpha = 0.3, fill = "#2b6cb0") +
  geom_line(aes(y = estimate), colour = "#2b6cb0") +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.1, 0.3)) +
  labs(x = "instances", y = "mean(loss_a - loss_b)") + theme_minimal()
```

## Louvain versus Leiden {#sec-louvain}

The third application, frozen on 2026-09-25, compares two community-detection algorithms whose
outputs tie, cluster and skew. Instances are stochastic block models with 3 to 6 blocks of
unequal sizes, 80 to 300 nodes and per-instance mixing; A is `cluster_louvain()` of
\pkg{igraph}, B `cluster_leiden()` run to convergence on modularity, both with the instance's
seed; the loss is $1 - Q$ with bounds $[0, 1.5]$, and $\delta = 0.01$ (one modularity point).
Its 100 replications are fresh streams of up to 6,000 instances, so the truth is known only
through a Monte Carlo reference of 5,000 instances, which puts the mean difference at 0.0055
in favour of Leiden, inside the margin. The per-instance differences are far from Gaussian:
40% exact ties, Louvain ahead in 3.5% of the instances, skewness 1.8. All four procedures
declared practical equivalence in every replication: the betting sequence after a median of
2,533 instances, empirical Bernstein after 5,090, the fixed-sample test at its limit of 6,000,
and the \pkg{safestats} sequence after a median of 26. That last number is not a success. On
this distribution the Gaussian sequence, designed with a pilot standard deviation, stopped
after 4 or 5 instances whenever the first differences were all ties, with an interval that had
collapsed to a point, and its running interval excluded the reference mean in 15% of the
replications, against none for the two bounded boundaries. The declaration happened to be
right because the truth is equivalence, but the guarantee was gone. Algorithm outputs tie,
cluster and skew, and a sequence that assumes a model pays for its speed in coverage exactly
where the assumption fails.

Two earlier applications, a location-estimator comparison and a knapsack heuristic comparison,
remain in `experiments/` with their frozen configurations; they show nothing the three above do
not.

# Potential uses {#sec-uses}

The protocol applies wherever two procedures are compared on a stream of independent units with
bounded, paired losses and the cost of each unit matters. We see five families of use.

- **Monte Carlo studies in statistics.** Comparing two estimators, tests or interval procedures
  by simulation is a benchmark whose instances are i.i.d. by construction, so (A1) holds
  exactly. The package then answers the question that fixed replication counts leave open:
  when can the study stop?
- **Operations research and optimisation.** Heuristics, metaheuristics and solver settings
  compared on an instance generator, as in the routing application of [Section 6](#sec-apps). A natural loss is a gap to
  a bound, which is bounded by construction, and the cost column can be CPU time or objective
  evaluations.
- **Regression testing of numerical software.** A new release of a solver against the previous
  one on a generator of test problems, inside continuous integration: an equivalence
  declaration is a statement of "no relevant regression" at a known error level, and an
  inconclusive outcome is a reason to look, not a pass.
- **Simulation-based policy evaluation.** Epidemic interventions ([Section 6](#sec-apps)),
  traffic control, inventory and supply-chain policies evaluated in stochastic simulators or
  digital twins. Scenarios drawn from a prior are the instances, stochastic replications are
  the seeds, and outcomes such as attack rates, service levels or fill rates are bounded
  proportions.
- **Machine learning evaluation.** Two models scored on i.i.d. test examples with a bounded
  per-example loss (zero-one loss, a capped log loss, a rubric score of a generated answer),
  where labelling or grading each example is expensive. Cross-validation folds are not
  independent instances [@nadeau2003]; the protocol applies to a held-out stream, not to
  folds.

Racing for algorithm configuration [@birattari2002] is a sequence of such comparisons; one
pairwise race with \pkg{seqbench} is valid, but a race among many candidates needs a
multiplicity correction or sequential model confidence sets [@arnold2026].

# Limitations and open problems {#sec-limitations}

**What it costs.** Distribution-free validity for bounded losses is expensive when the losses
have a small variance relative to their range: the Gaussian sequence with a known variance
needed `r sprintf("%.0f", 1 / max(sv_lo$ratio_to_betting))` to
`r sprintf("%.0f", 1 / min(sv_lo$ratio_to_betting))` times fewer instances at the low noise
level. The mechanism is the bet cap analysed in [Section 5](#sec-sim), and it implies a floor of
order $\log(1/\alpha)(b-a)/\big||\mu| - \delta\big|$ instances that does not vanish as the
variance shrinks. We conjecture that a floor of this order binds every procedure that is valid
for all distributions on $[a, b]$: a small contamination at an endpoint of the range changes
the mean while staying almost indistinguishable from the original distribution, which
suggests a change-of-measure lower bound. We have not proved it. Two levers are available now:
declare bounds as tight as the loss allows, because the cost scales with $b - a$, and raise the
bet cap towards 1. A declared variance bound helped little with the construction implemented in
the package: the `bernstein_declared` boundary needed 220 instances at the low-noise null where
betting with $c = 0.9$ needed 222 (968 against 385 at the high-noise null), because Bennett's
bound keeps a range term of order $\log(2/\alpha)/t$. This is a property of the Bennett
construction, not a proved limit, and whether one can do markedly better on bounded data with a
known variance bound is open. The Gaussian sequence escapes the floor by assuming a model;
it kept its coverage in the routing and vaccination applications, where the effects were large,
and lost it in the Louvain--Leiden application ([Section 6](#sec-apps)), where the paired
differences tie and skew and the truth lies inside the margin.

**What it does not claim.** The error control is a margin rule on an existing confidence
sequence, which a user who knows what to do could obtain from \pkg{safestats} or from the
constructions of @choe2024; sequential equivalence testing with e-values, including
data-dependent margins, is developed by @koobs2026. The package's contribution is the protocol,
its refusals, its contract and the accounting of cost.

**Scope.** The current version has the following limits.

- *Two algorithms.* Comparisons among $k > 2$ need a multiplicity correction or sequential
  model confidence sets [@hansen2011; @arnold2026].
- *A population target.* The estimand is the mean over a population of instances. Fixed
  benchmark suites such as public instance libraries are not random samples from anything; for
  them a finite-population target with sampling without replacement [@waudbysmith2020] is the
  right one, and it is not implemented.
- *Independent, exchangeable instances.* Instances that arrive in time, such as daily
  operations or production traffic, may drift or be serially dependent, which violates (A1);
  the package cannot detect this.
- *Bounded losses.* A loss must have known bounds. Unbounded losses must be bounded by the
  user, by truncation or penalisation, which changes the estimand, and wide bounds cost
  instances in proportion to their width.
- *A single, pre-specified margin and loss.* A trade-off between solution quality and
  running time must be folded into one loss before the study; the margin cannot be revised
  after inspection [@koobs2026 discuss post-hoc margins].
- *A mean.* A mean difference can hide heterogeneity: in the vaccination pool the mean
  benefit of degree targeting ranges from `r sprintf("%.3f", min(a12$mu))` in
  `r a12$label[which.min(a12$mu)]` networks to `r sprintf("%.3f", max(a12$mu))` in
  `r a12$label[which.max(a12$mu)]` networks. Subgroup questions need their own pre-registered
  comparisons.
- *Seeds fixed in advance.* Allocating more seeds to instances that look close is refused,
  not modelled, so the package cannot exploit adaptive designs within an instance. With the
  default boundary, extra seeds rarely pay unless the decision falls in the variance-driven
  regime (Sections [5](#sec-sim) and [6](#sec-apps)).
- *Implementation.* The betting boundary stores the history of observations, so memory grows
  linearly with the stream, and its reported endpoints between calls are outer grid edges, at
  most one grid cell (0.002 loss units on bounds $[0, 1]$ with the default grid) wider per side
  than the exact set.

# Summary {#sec-summary}

\pkg{seqbench} turns an algorithm comparison into a pre-registered sequential experiment with
an anytime-valid guarantee, a margin of practical equivalence and an explicit account of cost.
Its guarantee held in every simulated cell and application, the repeatedly inspected
$t$-test it replaces did not, and the price of distribution-free validity is reported rather
than hidden. Version 0.1.0 is on CRAN;^[<https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=seqbench>] the
version described here (0.1.1) and every configuration and analysis script used in this
article are on GitHub,^[<https://github.com/castlaboratory/seqbench>] and the documentation, with vignettes and
the two new case studies, is on the package site.^[<https://castlaboratory.github.io/seqbench/>]
